prompt: What does each line of `cases/dev.jsonl` hold?
hint: Two parts.

choices.text: A message and a person's answer
choices.why: Right: the answer a person decided was right. Everything after that is arithmetic.

choices.text: A message and the model's reply to it, saved the first time the prompt ran
choices.why: Replies go in `runs/`; the case holds the person's answer.

choices.text: A prompt and the message it was written for
choices.why: Prompts live in `prompts/`.

choices.text: A message and its cost in tokens
choices.why: Cost is computed from runs, not stored in cases.

prompt: Why write each label before running the prompt on the message?
hint: What changes once you have seen the model's answer?

choices.text: The harness refuses a case whose label was added after a run
choices.why: Nothing in the harness checks when a label was written.

choices.text: Labels written later cost more tokens
choices.why: Labels are not sent to the model.

choices.text: Afterwards you judge whether its answer is acceptable
choices.why: Right: an easier test than deciding what the message is about.

choices.text: So the model cannot read the label
choices.why: The model never sees `expect` either way.

prompt: `v4` passes 34 of 40 and `v3` passes 36. The sign test on the four messages that changed gives p = 0.625. What does that say?
hint: How often would a coin split four that unevenly?

choices.text: `v3` is better, by two messages
choices.why: Two messages is well within what chance produces.

choices.text: Forty cases cannot tell these two apart
choices.why: Right. A coin would do at least that more than half the time.

choices.text: `v4` is better, because the p-value is above 0.5
choices.why: A p-value does not point at a winner.

choices.text: The test set has a wrong label
choices.why: Nothing here suggests one.

prompt: A set of 40 cases sees differences of about ten points. Roughly how many cases would it take to see differences half that size?
hint: Noise shrinks with the square root of the count.

prompt: Put `pl check`'s checks in the order they run.
hint: Cheapest and most certain first.

prompt: Which checks could run on every reply in production, where no person has labelled the message?
hint: Which ones need `expect`?

choices.text: Only `category` and `urgency`
choices.why: Those are exactly the two that need a label.

choices.text: All five
choices.why: Two need the person's answer.

choices.text: `json`, `fields` and `labels`
choices.why: Right: they need only the reply and the specification.

choices.text: None of them: checks belong in the test set and nowhere else
choices.why: Lesson 10 used `json` on live replies to refuse injected ones.

prompt: `t03` failed `json`. Why is it not also listed as a wrong category?
hint: What happens after the first failure?

choices.text: Its category was right
choices.why: Nobody can tell: the reply could not be read.

choices.text: The list shows only the first check each reply failed
choices.why: Right, which makes it a list of first causes.

choices.text: Category is only checked at temperature 0
choices.why: Temperature does not change which checks run.

choices.text: `--failures` hides category failures unless asked
choices.why: It shows them; `t37` is listed under category in v3.

prompt: Which of these make a check worth having, according to the section? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four properties.

choices.text: It gives the same verdict every time
choices.why: Yes: a check that changes its mind is a second thing to measure.

choices.text: It is as strict as the program that reads the reply
choices.why: Yes, or it passes replies the program will refuse.

choices.text: It checks several properties at once, to save time
choices.why: One property each, so a failure says what failed.

choices.text: Its failure says what it saw
choices.why: Yes: *urgency normal, expected low* is a to-do item.

prompt: Why does `v3-examples.txt` pass 36 of 40 on `dev.jsonl` and only 11 of 30 on `holdout.jsonl`?
hint: Who wrote each set, and when?

choices.text: The holdout was run at a higher temperature
choices.why: Both runs were at temperature 0.

choices.text: Holdout replies stopped being valid JSON halfway through
choices.why: All 30 parse; the sorting fails.

choices.text: Dev was written by the prompt's author
choices.why: Right, and the holdout came later, from harder messages. Dev measured the messages its author imagined.

choices.text: The holdout's labels were written carelessly
choices.why: Nothing suggests that; the messages are harder.

prompt: `v3` beat `v4` on dev by 36 to 34, and they tie at 11 on the holdout. What does that suggest?
hint: A choice made on one set, checked on another.

choices.text: The holdout is too small to be used for anything
choices.why: Small, but it is exactly the check the dev score could not give.

choices.text: `v4` is the better prompt after all
choices.why: A tie says neither.

choices.text: Choosing by dev bought nothing visible
choices.why: Right: what made `v3` better on dev does not show elsewhere.

choices.text: Dev and the holdout measure the same thing
choices.why: Then they would not differ by 90% against 37%.

prompt: A second set, built apart and run only when deciding, so that it is never tuned against, is called a ___ set.
hint: You hold it back.

prompt: After shipping, you read why `h01` fails, change the prompt until it passes, and report the new holdout score. What is wrong with that number?
hint: What did `h01` become when you fixed it?

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the fix to the prompt is small
choices.why: Size does not matter; the prompt was fitted to that case.

choices.text: The holdout is now a second dev set
choices.why: Right, and you need a new holdout.

choices.text: It should be reported out of 29 instead of 30
choices.why: Removing one case does not undo the fitting.

choices.text: Holdout scores have to be run at temperature 1
choices.why: Temperature is unrelated.

prompt: `v11-contaminated.txt` uses `t21`, `t23` and `t37` as its examples. What happens to those three cases?
hint: The prompt contains their answers.

choices.text: They fail, because the model is confused by seeing them twice
choices.why: All three pass.

choices.text: They cannot fail any more, so they measure nothing
choices.why: Right: they are answered by copying.

choices.text: They are skipped by the harness
choices.why: Nothing in the harness notices.

choices.text: They cost no tokens
choices.why: They cost the same as any message.

prompt: On the 37 dev messages that are not its examples, how many does `v11-contaminated.txt` pass?
hint: It passes 37 of 40, and three of the 37 are its own examples.

prompt: Contamination raised the dev score by only one point here. Why is a small rise the dangerous kind?
hint: What does a one-point rise look like after somebody improved the examples?

choices.text: It looks like ordinary progress
choices.why: Right: nothing about it announces a leak.

choices.text: Small rises are never significant
choices.why: Significance is not the issue; the cases measure nothing.

choices.text: It makes the holdout score fall
choices.why: The holdout went from 11 to 12 here.

choices.text: One point is the most contamination can ever add
choices.why: It adds as many as leaked cases that were failing.

prompt: Two runs of the same prompt at temperature 1, with different seeds, passed 31 and 28. How many messages changed result between them?
hint: `fixed` plus `broken`.

prompt: At temperature 1, `t14` failed five calls of five. What kind of finding is that?
hint: Did it pass at temperature 0?

choices.text: A flaky case that needs more samples to measure
choices.why: It never changes; there is nothing to sample.

choices.text: A stable defect, in the prompt or in the label
choices.why: Right: one run finds it, at any temperature.

choices.text: Proof that temperature 1 is too high for this task
choices.why: It fails at temperature 0 too.

choices.text: Bad luck in the draw
choices.why: Five of five, and the same at temperature 0, is not luck.

prompt: A test that passes and fails the same input on different calls is called ___.
hint: Programmers' word for it.

prompt: Match each observation to what it tells you.
hint: One each.

pairs.left: A case fails every call, at any temperature
pairs.right: A defect in the prompt or the label

pairs.left: A case fails some calls and passes others
pairs.right: A rate, which only samples can measure

pairs.left: The dev score rises by one after examples are added
pairs.right: Check the examples are not test cases
The dev set is easier than real traffic

right_distractors: The checks run in the wrong order

prompt: A colleague reports: "New prompt: 38/40 on dev, up from 36. Ship it." The prompt runs at temperature 0.7 and was tuned on dev. What do you ask for first?
hint: Three things in this lesson could each produce those two points.

choices.text: A rerun of the same command, to confirm the 38
choices.why: One more run is one more draw; it says little.

choices.text: Rates over samples for both prompts, the holdout, and a check that no example is a dev case
choices.why: Right: flakiness, tuning and contamination each fake a gain.

choices.text: A larger dev set written by the same colleague
choices.why: More of the same author's messages keeps the same blind spot.

choices.text: The cost of the new prompt
choices.why: Worth knowing, but it does not test whether the gain is real.

prompt: Which of these is the strongest evidence that one prompt is better than another?
hint: Count what each result rests on.

choices.text: One run each on dev, three cases apart
choices.why: Two runs of one prompt differed by three here.

choices.text: Higher on the holdout, with a sign test well below 0.05
choices.why: Right: unseen cases, and a split a coin would rarely produce.

choices.text: Higher on dev after its examples were copied from dev
choices.why: Those cases measure nothing.

choices.text: Its author is confident
choices.why: Confidence is not a measurement.
